abstract: Reproduction imposes substantial energetic costs on female mammals, yet how females that show reduced overall energy expenditure adjust foraging to meet these demands remains incompletely understood. We examined two dimensions of behavioral response in female mantled howler monkeys (Alouatta palliata): feeding time (how much of the day, and how often, females feed) and foraging performance (the rate of dry matter intake when feeding occurs). We tested three hypotheses: (H1) females maintain stable feeding time and stable intake rate across reproductive states; (H2) females maintain stable feeding time but elevate intake rate during gestation and lactation; (H3) females reduce feeding time and do not elevate intake rate. Using 3,765 focal observations from 11 females across ten years, we classified reproductive state as cycling, gestating, early, mid, or late lactation, or concurrent gestation with lactation. Feeding time declined during reproduction: early lactating, mid-lactating, and concurrent females allocated approximately 15, 16, and 29 fewer minutes per day to feeding than cycling females, and the probability of feeding during a focal sample fell by 6.1 and 7.4 percentage points in early and mid lactation. Foraging performance did not vary: when females fed, intake rate, total intake, and diet composition were comparable across states. These results support H3. Combined with parallel evidence from this population that lactating females increase resting rather than feeding time and show no elevation of dry matter intake during lactation, our findings suggest that female mantled howlers meet reproductive costs primarily by drawing on capital reserves rather than through behavioral compensation.
title: Eating Smart When Time Is Short: Stable Performance Despite Reduced Feeding Time During Reproduction in Mantled Howlers
Hormonal control and signaling of the testis of the bat Molossus molossus during the processes of testicular maturation, regression, and recrudescence

abstract: ABSTRACT In speech signal processing, noise interference during transmission or recording remains a persistent challenge. To address this, we propose a hybrid denoising method combining Grey Wolf Optimizer‐Variational Mode Decomposition (GWO‐VMD) with Tunable‐Q Wavelet Transform (TQWT). First, the GWO algorithm is utilized to optimize the VMD decomposition parameter combination, specifically the number of modes and the penalty factor. Based on the correlation coefficient screening principle, the Intrinsic Mode Function (IMF) components with relatively low correlation coefficients are then removed. Next, the remaining IMFs are recombined, and multi‐scale analysis is conducted through TQWT. Finally, the sub‐band components whose relative energy exceeds a certain threshold are reconstructed to obtain the denoised signal. For the original three‐segment noisy speech signals, the signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) has been remarkably enhanced by using the GWO‐VMD‐TQWT denoising method. It has increased from −1.2227, 8.4398, −4.6318 to 11.4980, 19.2606, 6.1067 dB, respectively. Additionally, the root mean square error of this algorithm after denoising is the smallest among the compared methods. Evidently, the joint denoising method in this study outperforms single VMD, TQWT, and classical denoising techniques like EMD, EWT, and CEEMDAN. It provides an effective solution for low SNR speech signal denoising.
journal: Concurrency and Computation Practice and Experience
title: Speech Signal Denoising Based on GWO ‐ VMD Combined With TQWT

abstract: Abstract The human‐built environment influences the behavior and survival of many species, but most of these studies have been conducted in urban areas. Yet, anthropogenic development may impact species differently across scales, including at the rural level. We examined whether the built environment in a rural area obstructed visibility and influenced the antipredator behaviors of yellow‐bellied marmots ( Marmota flaviventer ). We collected observational and experimental data around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado, USA, to analyze differences in maximum running speed, antipredator vigilance, propensity to alarm call, and flight initiation distance at both undeveloped and low human density developed sites. We calculated marmot viewscapes using high‐resolution light detection and ranging (LiDAR) scans of marmot colonies and conducted visibility analyses to understand how overall visibility influences antipredator behaviors. We used mixed models to analyze the relationship between antipredator behaviors, development, and visibility. Development and visibility interacted to affect marmot vigilance: Animals in developed sites with highly variable visibility allocated more time to vigilance than animals in undeveloped, highly variable visibility sites, suggesting that despite the benefits of the human shield effect, living in close proximity to humans may increase risk perceptions more than living in undeveloped areas that had a similar level of visibility. We found no association between different intensities of development and visibility with maximum running speed, alarm calling propensity, or flight initiation distance. However, we found that marmots living in areas with highly variable visibility were less likely to emit alarm calls. We conclude that visibility analyses may be effective at explaining variation in some, but not all, antipredator behaviors. Our study provides a comprehensive and mechanistic examination of the ways in which human disturbance may affect behaviors with documented fitness consequences. We encourage continued consideration and study of human disturbance's impacts on wildlife behavior at the rural scale.
title: Investigating the relationship between antipredator behavior and human disturbance using LiDAR imagery

title: Eyes, ears, and play in the wild: flexible use of sensory channels in spotted hyena communication

abstract: Insectivorous bats navigate mainly by echolocation, but may also use visual, olfactory, and magnetic cues when travelling long distances. Parsing the relative contributions of different senses for navigation is difficult in wild bats. In the lab, spatial navigation in rodents is often studied using different maze assays, including the widely employed multiple T-mazes. Here, we trained crawling Mexican free-tailed bats (Tadarida brasiliensis) to navigate a multiple T-maze within an artificial magnetic field and then manipulated the sensory environment to quantify the relative importance of vision, hearing and magnetic field cues on their navigation performance. We predicted that in addition to echolocation, visual and geomagnetic sensory cues might provide significant contributions to bat navigation performance. We hypothesized that (1) randomly reversing the polarity of the magnetic field, (2) changing color or removing light from the arena, or (3) presenting an acoustic jamming stimulus would increase mean maze travel times. Results showed that reversing the magnetic field had no significant impact on maze travel times under any conditions. However, in total darkness, mean travel times increased by 75% relative to both broad spectrum white light and red light. Travel times under red light were longer but not significantly different from white light. Playing an acoustic jamming stimulus mimicking the pulses of other bats significantly increased mean travel times by ~ 50%. These results show that insectivorous bats supplement biosonar with visual cues during navigation, but we found no evidence of a contribution from magnetoreception.
title: Echolocating free-tailed bats use vision and hearing but not magnetoreception when navigating a maze

abstract: Abstract Vocal displays play a key role in mediating intergroup competition among primates, yet the mechanisms through which these signals influence contest outcomes remain unclear. In this study, we investigated close-range vocal encounters among six groups of black howler monkeys ( Alouatta pigra ) in Palenque National Park, Mexico. We used acoustic recordings of 58 intergroup vocal duels. We examined how structural and social features of howling bouts predict success in contests over resources. Our predictors captured three components of vocal interactions: participation (number and identity of callers), synchrony (their temporal alignment), and temporal position (which group initiated or ended the bout and which produced the longest sequence). Bayesian generalized linear mixed models revealed that specific elements of the temporal organization of vocal interactions strongly influenced the likelihood of winning. Groups were more successful when they ended the bout, when adult males terminated simultaneously, when at least one female contributed, when sequences were longer, and when the first call was a roar. Drawn encounters invariably triggered subsequent vocal duels, underscoring the role of repeated signaling in conflict resolution. These findings show that howler monkeys use coordinated and strategically structured vocal behavior as reliable indicators of motivation and cohesion, supporting assessment strategies that reduce costly physical conflicts. Our results highlight the importance of collective motivation, coordination, and persistence of contributions in shaping the dynamics of intergroup competition in primates.
title: Beyond the Final Say: Social Coordination Shapes Success in Howler Monkey (Alouatta pigra) Vocal Duels

abstract: Abstract Echolocation is a biological adaptation that can be influenced by body mass (Mb). To cope with seasonal changes in ambient temperature (Ta) and food availability, bats either increase Mb to hibernate or reduce it to remain active during winter and minimize energy expenditure. In bats that remain active throughout the year, seasonal changes in Mb may affect echolocation traits. We analyzed Mb and echolocation pulses of Eptesicus fuscus captured in La Malinche National Park, a montane ecosystem in central Mexico, during the dry-cold and dry-warm seasons. We examined the relationship between Mb, season and Ta, and four echolocation variables: maximum frequency, peak frequency, minimum frequency, and bandwidth. Our results revealed a positive relationship between Mb and season and Ta, and a negative relationship between Mb and all four echolocation variables. These findings suggest that seasonal variation in echolocation traits, associated to changes in Mb, has important ecological implications enabling bats to adjust to changing prey availability. During the dry-warm season, larger bats with lower frequencies and narrower bandwidths may reduce acoustic resolution without substantially compromising foraging efficiency in prey-rich environments. In contrast smaller bats with higher-resolution calls may enhance prey detection when sources are limited during the dry-cold season. Future avenues of research on this topic are discussed.
title: Seasonal shifts in body mass shape echolocation traits in Eptesicus fuscus from central Mexico
Development and evaluation of two colloidal gold lateral flow test strips for large Yellow Croaker Iridovirus (LYCIV) detection

abstract: Vocal production learning is known to occur in a limited number of non-human taxa. Among birds, songbirds such as Zebra Finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ) are often studied as closed-ended learners, acquiring their vocal repertoire only during an early sensitive period, whereas open-ended learners like parrots can acquire new vocalizations throughout life. However, relatively little attention was paid to learning process of open-ended learners at different developmental stages. Whether open-ended learners such as Budgerigars ( Melopsittacus undulatus ) maintain high-level vocal learning ability into adulthood remains underexplored. Here, we investigated age-related differences in vocal learning capacity in Budgerigars by comparing their ability to learn human speech sounds at different ages. We found that the capacity to learn human vocalizations was retained into early adulthood. However, compared with juveniles, young adults showed a lower probability of successful learning and reduced overall imitation similarity within the training period. Interestingly, young adults exhibited significantly higher temporal order similarity in vocal output than juveniles. Nevertheless, birds aged 3–4 years old were unable to learn human speech sounds. These findings revealed that while Budgerigars are open-ended learners, their vocal learning ability declined with age. These results provide experimental evidence for understanding open-ended vocal learning and its changes at different developmental stages, and offer insights for comparative studies of human speech learning.
title: Vocal learning in juvenile and adult Budgerigars
IRS-UAV assisted military communications in mountainous NLOS environments: A hybrid metaheuristic anti-jamming strategy

abstract: Congestion management is a crucial aspect of maintaining stability and efficiency in modern power grids, particularly as networks expand and dynamic conditions evolve. This paper presents an adaptive congestion management approach using Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) and Multi-Agent System (MAS) based communication for optimal power dispatch. The methodology is validated on the IEEE 57-bus system, where a manager agent coordinates with generator agents to iteratively adjust power outputs while ensuring economic load dispatch (ELD) and minimizing congestion. The system employs Smart Python Agent Development Environment (SPADE) based decentralized communication over an XMPP Openfire server, allowing seamless coordination among agents. A comparative analysis with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) highlights the limitations of PSO in resolving congestion in large-scale networks, demonstrating the superior effectiveness of GWO in handling transmission constraints and improving Available Transfer Capability (ATC). The results show that the proposed GWO-MAS approach achieves lower generation costs, better congestion mitigation, and enhanced grid flexibility. This research reveals the potential of bio-inspired optimization for adaptive and decentralized congestion management in smart grids and future power networks.
title: Adaptive Congestion Management in Power Grids Using Grey Wolf Optimization and Multi-Agent Communication

abstract: The ongoing expansion of human enterprise into remote environments has contributed to degradation and fragmentation of ecosystems globally, reducing plant and animal species’ habitats and viability. Western North America’s sagebrush ecosystems have been reduced to half the area of their historical range, largely driven by anthropogenic activities. A relatively recent advancement has been the rapid construction of wireless communication infrastructure. While modern communication technology is essential for economic progress and critical to rural communities, its associated infrastructure may have undesired influences on sagebrush ecosystems and associated wildlife. However, such influences, along with their potential remediation to benefit species conservation, are poorly understood. We investigated the effects of communication tower infrastructure over 25 years (1996–2020) on the greater sage-grouse ( Centrocercus urophasianus ; hereafter, sage-grouse), a species of conservation concern often considered to be an indicator for the health of sagebrush ecosystems. We used hierarchical population state-space models coupled with male lek counts to investigate spatiotemporal effects of towers on sage-grouse annual rate of change ( λ ˆ ) in apparent abundance while considering influences of other anthropogenic infrastructure and environmental characteristics at multiple spatial scales. Both tower density and proximity were negatively related to λ ˆ up to 12.5 km away from tower sites. Higher elevation and sagebrush cover positively influenced λ ˆ while tree cover and annual grass cover exhibited negative associations. We used model results to inform a decision support framework that could guide location siting of future communication infrastructure based on minimization of effects to sage-grouse populations. Increases in communication tower infrastructure was one of the factors contributing to a ~1.6% overall decrease in expected λ ˆ during the study, but simulations demonstrated how placing infrastructure away from sage-grouse breeding areas could minimize negative effects. Our findings, coupled with decision support analyses, can help inform local, regional, and national conservation strategies that seek to minimize or mitigate undesired effects of communication infrastructure.
title: A model-based decision support framework for siting communication tower infrastructure to reduce adverse effects on a sagebrush-obligate species
The transcriptional regulator Sfa4 controls H4-T6SS expression and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa through FleQ and c-di-GMP signaling

abstract: Recognizing other individuals across multiple sensory modalities is important for animals in social groups. Processing of multisensory information is shaped by social and sensory experiences, especially early in development. Zebra finches form lasting pair-bonds and recognize their partners acoustically and visually. However, the degree to which multisensory integration or developmental experience shape recognition is unclear. We tested female responses to audiovisual stimuli where audio and video of familiar (partner) or unfamiliar birds was congruent (e.g., familiar audio and familiar video) or incongruent (e.g., familiar audio and unfamiliar video). Using automated pose-tracking, we found that stimulus congruency affected behavior, with females showing more head turning and vocalizations to mismatched audio and video. While both colony-reared birds and birds reared without exposure to adult song detected audiovisual congruency, they differed in the degree of their behaviors. Thus, female finches integrate multisensory information for partner identification, but differences in developmental environment influence behavioral expression.
title: Rearing condition affects behavioral response to cross-modal expectancy violation paradigm in zebra finches

abstract: Given the widespread concern over university students' psychological health and the significant role of biological sounds in psychological recovery, this study experimentally verified the effects of forest park biological sounds on stressed university students. We recruited 32 students (stress measured via the Perceived Stress Scale), used 11 biological sound samples from Henan forest parks as auditory stimuli, and tested their electroencephalogram (EEG) and psychological questionnaire in the laboratory. We find that biological sounds enhance security/relaxation and alleviate fatigue, with stronger effects in highly stressed students; Oecanthus indicus Saussure, Hirundo rustic , and Ardea intermedia exert the most positive effects, while Corvus macrorhynchos and Tettigonia chinensis Willemse have negative effects; Hirundo rustica , Oecanthus indicus Saussure, and Passer ammodendri score highest in psychological perception; and psychological and physiological responses correlate significantly. These findings highlight bioacoustics' value in relieving student stress and provide data for future forest park landscape and soundscape design.
title: Effects of forest park’s biological sounds on the positive responses of stressed university student

abstract: Social interaction facilitates vocal learning more effectively than passive exposure, but the neural signals that reflect the social context of auditory experience remain unclear. Midbrain dopaminergic circuits broadcast motivational and learning-related signals, raising the possibility that VTA/SNc activity may reflect both tutor-song auditory input and tutor presence during juvenile vocal development. We tested this idea in juvenile zebra finches by recording single-unit activity during the same tutor-song playback under tutor-absent and tutor-present conditions; in the tutor-present condition, a live tutor was present but remained silent. Among 185 VTA/SNc neurons from 8 birds, tutor presence bidirectionally modulated auditory responses. Type-1 neurons showed enhancement (46/185, 24.9%), whereas Type-2 neurons showed suppression (29/185, 15.7%). Both profiles were observed in all birds, and bird-level analyses supported consistent modulation. Type-1 neurons showed increased baseline firing and a further enhancement of baseline-subtracted song-evoked responses, whereas Type-2 suppression occurred without reduced baseline firing. Using spike waveform and firing rate criteria, we found that the tutor-enhanced Type-1 population included neurons with putative dopaminergic features. In naturalistic recordings, these neurons also showed increased activity during live tutor singing. These findings suggest that socially modulated VTA/SNc activity may link tutor presence to auditory processing relevant to vocal learning.
title: Social context bidirectionally modulates VTA/SNc responses to tutor song in juvenile zebra finches

abstract: Chronic stress affects cognitive function across many domains, including memory, decision making and learning. While the effects of early-life stress on vocal learning in juveniles are well-demonstrated in both humans and songbirds, less is known about how stress experienced by adults affects their ability to learn new vocalizations or the neural substrates that underlie this behavior. We investigated the effects of chronic stress on the production and learning of contact calls, and on the expression of a key learning related gene, FoxP2, in the vocal learning circuit in adult budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus), a small parrot with open-ended vocal learning. We induced chronic stress via unpredictable disturbances in the captive environments of nine newly-formed replicate flocks of 4 adult male budgerigars who were previously unfamiliar to each other. We then recorded calling behavior daily and measured weight, breath rate, and baseline and stress response levels of circulating corticosterone weekly. At the end of the experiment brains were collected to examine mRNA and protein levels of the gene FoxP2 in the vocal learning region magnocellular nucleus of the medial striatum (MMSt) using qPCR and immunohistochemistry. Physiological measures of stress consistently showed stronger responses in birds subjected to the highest level of disturbance than those in the medium or baseline control treatments, although only differences in baseline corticosterone were detected among treatments. We used machine learning approaches to map calls onto a shared acoustic space to assess four measures of vocal behavior and learning: vocal output (the number of contact calls produced), vocal diversity (the amount of acoustic space occupied by the calls of an individual), vocal plasticity (the amount of change in acoustic space over time) and vocal convergence (the degree of overlap between an individual's calls and the calls of its group). Birds in the high stress treatment showed higher vocal output and lower vocal plasticity than those in medium stress or baseline control groups, but there were no differences among treatments in vocal diversity or vocal convergence. There were no differences detected among treatments in expression levels of either FoxP2 mRNA or protein, perhaps due to the timing of neural sampling relative to the behavioral measures. These results suggest that, as seen in juvenile learning, chronic stress can negatively impact vocal learning in adults via changes in patterns of circulating corticosterone.
title: Chronic stress raises baseline circulating corticosterone and reduces vocal plasticity in male budgerigars, an avian model for adult vocal learning

abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a diverse class of short peptides with therapeutic potential as antimicrobial agents and immune regulators. Many anurans (frogs and toads) produce diverse sets of AMPs via specialized skin glands, yet their biological significance remains debated. To better understand the evolution and expression of anuran AMPs, we examined the Wood Frog (Rana sylvatica) genome, assembled a skin transcriptome to identify skin-secreted AMP genes, and confirmed the presence of predicted AMPs in skin secretions using mass spectrometry. Along with discovering nine novel AMPs, we found that the AMP genes of R. sylvatica cluster in a manner similar to other AMP gene families and that analogous gene clusters appear in other Rana species and more distant relatives. These genes possess a consistent structure, and all encode a conserved signal peptide which is subject to strong purifying selection, contrasting with the varied associated AMPs. We examined the effects of season and pathogen exposure on AMP gene expression, observing large differences in transcript and peptide levels between genes. Overall, our findings provide insight into broad patterns of AMP evolution in anurans, reinforcing the importance of the signal peptide as a functional feature of skin-secreted peptide precursors which requires further study.
title: The Rana sylvatica skin-secreted antimicrobial peptide (AMP) gene repertoire highlights broader patterns in anuran AMP evolution

abstract: Bats evolved the ability to echolocate prey in night sky, but this dark and quiet sensory niche is increasingly encroached upon by anthropogenic light and noise pollution. Here, we test the hypotheses that such pollutions displace bats from their foraging sites and that the displacement increases with stressor intensity. To do so we exposed wild Daubenton's bats (Myotis daubentonii) to controlled levels of light or ultrasonic broad-band noise and recorded bat activity levels via passive acoustic monitoring at different distances to the stressors. We find that light-, and noise-exposures reduced bat activity by 43% and 49% respectively compared to control periods within 6m of the stressor source. The displacement effect decreased with increasing distance to the light and noise sources. At 20m from the source, light levels of 1 Lux still exerted a modest reduction in bat activity. By contrast, at 20 m, noise levels of 56 dB re. 20μPa RMS no longer elicited a measurable displacement of bats. We conclude that moderate anthropogenic light- and noise pollution can displace bats from their foraging sites and that light and ultrasonic noise pollution should be mitigated around critical bat habitats.
title: Light and ultrasonic noise pollution displaces trawling Daubenton’s bats

abstract: Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate multidimensional cues or prioritize a single dimension when processing multidimensional input. We investigated how humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) process concurrent acoustic cues using an identical behavioural paradigm with complex-tone sequences. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these processing strategies. We show that zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance on pitch. Experience further modulates this bias, with trained human listeners recruiting secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch is unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience-dependent functional substitution.
title: Divergent processing strategies for auditory sequence recognition in humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)

abstract: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) has emerged as a powerful tool for passive whale monitoring, enabling both the detection of vocalizations and the simultaneous tracking of multiple individuals. However, a fundamental limitation of passive acoustic monitoring is that most methods rely on acoustic data, which is only available when whales vocalize. This clearly demonstrates the need for new sensing methods that can detect silent whales. In this paper, we detect hydrodynamic pressure and velocity fields in the low-frequency DAS data induced by a whale's motion and develop methods to analyze these signals. First, we use ships as proxies to demonstrate and calibrate the proposed method. Then, we show that a simple fluid mechanical model can be adapted to understand how whale swimming can be detected and analyzed using DAS. We detect multiple silent whales simultaneously, estimate their characteristics, and show that whale motion signals decay as one over distance cubed. Moreover, we demonstrate that we can observe hydrodynamic pressure and velocity signals from a cruise ship at 413 m water depth, and up to 550 m from the fiber cable. In comparison, the smaller blue whales can be observed when diving within 40 m of the fiber-optical cable. This sensing method enables an approach to monitoring one of the world's most endangered species.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Detecting silent whales using seabed fiber-optic cables

abstract: Alarm calls, the vocalisations given during encounters with threats, vary tremendously in acoustic structure across species. Many alarm calls are structurally graded, which can convey information about predator type, urgency or proximity. However, graded variation is challenging to analyse with traditional categorical approaches. Here, we used fuzzy clustering to quantitatively classify and describe the alarm call repertoire of male Red-winged Blackbirds (Agelaius phoeniceus) in Michigan, U.S.A. We recorded calls from 74 males, generating a library of more than 13,000 vocalisations. We then selected 1,521 high-quality, non-overlapped calls for acoustic analysis and extracted 50 acoustic parameters per call. Using fuzzy k-means clustering, we identified the most stable number of call types, calculated membership values for primary and secondary clusters and developed thresholds that distinguish discrete, intermediate and graded call structures. Male Red-winged Blackbirds produced six alarm calls, check, cluck, zeer, seee, se-er and ti-er, which varied in the extent to which they share acoustic features. Cluck calls were discrete, whereas zeer, seee, se-er and ti-er formed a graded continuum; check calls were intermediate. These findings reveal previously unmeasured variation and unrecognised complexity in the species’ alarm signalling system and demonstrate the value of fuzzy clustering for classifying graded vocal repertoires in animals.
title: Fuzzy clustering methods reveal structurally discrete and graded alarm calls in male Red-winged Blackbirds ( Agelaius phoeniceus )

abstract: Bush crickets (Insecta, Orthoptera, Ensifera) stridulate with their forewings to produce acoustic communication signals, known as songs. Studies analysing the relation between the morphology of their specialised wing structures and the songs produced are usually performed either at the intraspecific or interspecific level. Here, the differences between intra- and interspecific analyses are shown by combining multiple statistical analyses on acoustic and morphometric data compiled from six European bush cricket species. The analysis shows an overall trend for negative correlations between the size of wing regions and the fundamental frequency of the song. On an interspecific level, the area of the mirror and harp on both wings are good predictors for frequency, with the area of the left wing mirror having the highest predictive power. However, results on the interspecific level are not found within all species. Likewise, correlations found on an intraspecific level cannot be interpolated onto all species. This is exemplified using the newly introduced morphological trait circularity of wing regions. Only in Phaneroptera nana does the circularity of the elongated right wing mirror show a significant correlation with the fundamental frequency. The results illustrate potential problems of generalisation, like the occlusion of species-specific adaptations and high intraspecific variation.
title: Intra- and interspecific correlations between forewing morphology and sound production in six European bush cricket species (Tettigoniidae)

abstract: This conceptual paper develops and applies a Nonviolent Communication (NVC) framework to wildlife tourism, proposing it as a communication-based framework to help address human–wildlife conflict and advance biodiversity-relevant outcomes. NVC is a process designed to mediate disagreements and conflicts at all levels, utilising a language of compassion built around deep listening to others, respect, attentiveness, and empathy. The model is based on four key components: observations, feelings, needs, and requests, encompassing dialogue from all relevant stakeholders, including wildlife, local communities, tourists, tourism operators, and NGOs. We argue for the importance of teaching and literacy in nonviolent communication, both in theory and practice, as efforts to push the field in new directions while also keeping pace with developments in other disciplines. We apply the model to real-world examples of animal-based tourism, including camel riding in Australia, the Giant Panda Base in China, and bullfighting in Mexico. The framework extends existing welfare and coexistence models by positioning empathy as a structured and dialogic process through which interactions among tourism actors may be interpreted in relation to animal welfare, coexistence, and biodiversity concerns.
title: Nonviolent communication and the wildlife tourism sector

abstract: Abstract In the southwest Indian Ocean (SWIO), the Mascarene region has been identified as an Important Marine Mammals Area, yet the seasonal use of these waters by large baleen whales remains poorly resolved. We analysed passive acoustic data from 16 Ocean Bottom Seismometers deployed from October 2012 to November 2013 across latitudinal and longitudinal transects around Réunion Island and off eastern Madagascar. Songs of fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia), and SWIO/Madagascar pygmy blue whales (B. m. brevicauda) were manually annotated from spectrograms to quantify hourly acoustic presence per day. Fin whales showed the highest acoustic presence among the three studied taxa, with seasonal presence lasting up to 8 months (April–December) and clear north–south patterns in the onset and end of acoustic presence. Antarctic blue whales were detected less frequently, primarily during austral autumn and winter, with records extending north to 16°S and secondary peaks in October–November consistent with southward movement after wintering farther north. Madagascar pygmy blue whales showed a pronounced bimodal acoustic presence (mid-October–mid-January; March–July/August) and a strong longitudinal structuring, with greater acoustic presence in the western part of the study area. The spatial distribution differed markedly between these two periods, revealing distinct migration pathways through the region during northward and southward movements. Taken together, these results identify the Mascarene waters as a shared seasonal habitat for fin whales, Antarctic blue whales, and Madagascar pygmy blue whales, while highlighting distinct seasonal and spatial patterns among taxa. Given the intense shipping activity in the region, continued and expanded acoustic monitoring is needed to assess long-term whale habitat use, characterize underwater noise, and evaluate its potential influence on the use of these waters, thereby informing future conservation measures.
title: Seasonal acoustic presence of blue and fin whales in the Mascarene waters (southwestern Indian Ocean)

abstract: To editor: Maternal death, often viewed through the narrow lens of immediate causes and medical prevention, carries collateral damage that extends profoundly beyond the individual woman. This damage, frequently unrecognized or forgotten, creates a lasting ripple effect on families, communities, and future generations. The loss of a mother is not merely a tragic statistic but a catastrophic event that alters the very fabric of social structures and emotional well-being.1 The concept of “collateral damage” refers to the unintended consequences of maternal death, manifest as deep trauma for surviving family members, economic instability, and loss of a nurturing figure for children. When a mother dies, her children are deprived of essential support, guidance, and care, leading to adverse outcomes in their physical, mental, and developmental health. Communities lose a vital contributor and face increased resource strains. Furthermore, this loss can exacerbate existing gender inequality and health disparities, as women often fulfill crucial caregiving and economic roles. Recognizing and addressing this forgotten collateral damage is essential for a holistic approach to maternal health that prioritizes the well-being and recovery of those left behind.2 The neglected consequences: biological and social impacts Emerging research highlights the profound, yet previously underexplored, biological and social consequences of maternal death. Studies in animal models, simulating maternal death through separation, have demonstrated significant alterations in the brain structure of offspring (Rattus norvegicus), including increased neural apoptosis, reduced neurotrophic support, and disrupted synaptic function.3 In humans, maternal death leads to a higher density of glucocorticoid receptors in the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex, increasing risk of neurodevelopment alteration in the future.4 Early maternal separation adversely affects offspring’s neurological growth and development, elevating the likelihood of psychiatric illnesses in adulthood, triggering neuroinflammatory reactions, and elevating the synthesis of inflammatory cytokines. These biological changes highlight the essential importance of maternal presence in early neurodevelopment, while proof of such changes in the human brain remains insufficient. Parallel human social studies emphasize the far-reaching consequences on families2: Impact on fathers and family: widowers often face overwhelming grief and unexpected, heavy caregiving responsibilities, which can significantly influence their parenting styles and remarriage decisions. Younger widowers or those with fewer children are often more engaged in active caregiving, while others may delegate responsibilities, highlighting the need for targeted support. Husbands and extended families grapple with psychological and financial burdens, especially in settings where women contribute significantly to household income. Impact on children: children under five who experience maternal death face a significantly increased risk of growth and developmental disorders, nutritional deficits, and school dropout due to the loss of essential maternal care and nurturing. Research shows that maternal death can increase the risk of developmental disorders in young children by a relative risk of 2.5. Especially for newborns, they are extremely vulnerable, often losing immediate access to breastfeeding and facing increased risks of malnutrition, infection, and mortality without maternal care. Global health efforts and the missing link Maternal mortality remains a critical global health issue, with approximately 287,000 women dying during and following pregnancy and childbirth in 2020. Alarmingly, nearly 95% of these deaths occur in low and lower-middle-income countries, largely due to preventable causes like hypertension and post-partum hemorrhage.1 Leading global organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO), United States Agency for International Development, Harvard University, and Johns Hopkins University, have initiated remarkable programs to reduce maternal mortality. Their efforts focus on prevention, such as strengthening emergency obstetric care, improving access to quality services, and setting strategic goals like the WHO’s Strategies toward Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality.5 However, a critical gap exists: these efforts primarily focus on prevention over aftermath. The specific operational guidance for managing the aftermath of maternal death and supporting families—such as that outlined by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, which emphasizes compassionate, structured support for partners, children, and staff—is often not fully integrated into broader frameworks. To truly address maternal health holistically, programs must evolve to include support for the resilience and recovery of the surviving family unit.6 Short-term effects: the void of sudden absence Maternal death instantly creates an emotional and physical void for the newborn. This sudden absence critically disrupts neural growth and bonding, impacting early attachment formation and the very structure of the developing brain. A crucial loss is the maternal voice, which functions not just as sound but as a developmental catalyst; its absence creates an emotional deficit that can hinder language acquisition, social interaction, and emotional regulation, delaying the formation of essential neural pathways. Compounding this trauma is biological stress: the event can trigger an elevation of stress hormones, particularly cortisol, in the newborn. Prolonged exposure to high cortisol levels interferes with brain regions vital for learning, memory, and emotional processing, significantly increasing the child’s risk of developing long-term mental health challenges.7,8 Long-term effects: the silent echo (epigenetic process) The child’s long-term health trajectory is silently but profoundly shaped by the circumstances following maternal death, a phenomenon explained through the Fetal Origins of Adult Disease and Developmental Origins of Health and Disease hypotheses. The disruption in the intrauterine environment, combined with subsequent suboptimal postnatal care, can lead to fetal programming, predisposing the newborn to chronic conditions later in life, such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases. Beyond physical health, the absence of early maternal bonding and nurturing has severe neurological and psychological consequences, such as increasing of cytokines production in the brain, impairs synaptic plasticity, and increasing of reactive oxydative species.9 Maternal separation often results in attachment disturbances, increased susceptibility to mental health disorders, and enduring behavioral challenges that affect the child’s cognitive and psychological well-being throughout their life. Addressing the forgotten damage: a call to action Maternal health must be viewed as an investment in the future of families and communities, not solely as a medical issue. Mitigating the profound collateral damage of maternal death requires a multifaceted, holistic approach that begins with early interventions and support. This includes implementing policies that provide targeted assistance, such as enhanced access to healthcare, mental health resources, and nutritional support specifically for bereaved caregivers and children. Furthermore, developing nurturing environments—through programs that foster emotional and interactive engagement for newborns and alternative caregivers—can partially bridge the gap left by maternal absence and promote healthy growth trajectories. This must be paired with holistic family support, establishing comprehensive programs that offer psychological counseling, financial aid, and resources for coping with emotional and economic challenges. Creating peer support networks for bereaved families and educating healthcare providers on the broader implications of maternal death are also vital components. Hence, programs for children growing up without a mother should be integrated into the primary program at community health centers and monitored by health educators to facilitate early problem detection. Finally, sustained effort requires policy and research by advocating for maternal health policies integrated into public health agendas, securing funding not only to reduce mortality but also to support affected families. Targeted research investment to explore the neurological and developmental consequences of maternal loss will further inform effective, compassionate interventions (Fig. 1).2,10Figure 1: We have to move from only root cause analysis to prevent future events to root cause analysis and mitigate the short and long-term impact of maternal death to the newborn, children, husband, and family.Conclusion The narrative surrounding maternal mortality must evolve to prioritize the well-being of the entire family unit. By acknowledging and addressing the forgotten collateral damage, we honor the memory of those who have died and commit to building a healthier, more equitable future for all families. We must move beyond only root cause analysis for prevention and equally commit to mitigating the short and long-term impact on the newborn, children, husband, and family. Additional research should be conducted to examine how children develop in the absence of their mothers. Funding None. Conflicts of Interest None. Data Availability All data generated or analyzed during this study are included in this published article.
title: The Forgotten Collateral Damage of Maternal Deaths

abstract: HYPOTHESIS: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a less invasive drug delivery device, the pyro-drive jet injector-intratympanic (PJI-IT), as an alternative to the conventional intratympanic injection (ITI). BACKGROUND: Conventional ITI using fine needles can cause damage to the tympanic membrane and hearing loss. A safer, less invasive delivery platform would be valuable for the local treatment of inner-ear disorders. METHODS: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) containing firefly luciferase (Fluc) mRNA were injected into the middle ears of male guinea pigs (n=30) using the needle-free PJI-IT, which created a small, temporary perforation of the tympanic membrane through a high-pressure liquid jet. Conventional fine [30-gauge (30G)] needle injection was used as control. Perforation size and closure time were measured microscopically. Bioluminescence imaging was performed to evaluate Fluc protein production. Auditory brainstem responses (ABRs) were recorded before and after the injection to assess auditory function. RESULTS: The PJI-IT and the 30G needle provided comparable amounts of Fluc protein in the tympanic cavity and cochlea. Compared with the conventional needle, the PJI-IT caused a smaller perforation of the tympanic membrane, which was closed faster. Auditory function was virtually preserved after injection using the PJI-IT, whereas injection using the conventional fine needle induced significant ABR threshold elevations. CONCLUSIONS: The PJI-IT has the potential to be a safe and minimally invasive instrument for intratympanic injections. The preserved auditory function and rapid healing of the perforated tympanic membrane suggest its clinical availability, especially for the repeated administration of biological agents such as mRNA regenerative medicine.
title: A Needle-Free Jet Injection System for Safe and Effective Intratympanic Delivery

abstract: HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that isolated changes in middle ear air volume do not increase the risk of diving-related middle ear barotrauma, and that Eustachian tube function is the primary determinant of barotrauma development. BACKGROUND: The relative contributions of middle ear air volume and Eustachian tube function to the development of diving-related middle ear barotrauma remain controversial. This first experimental comparative study aimed to differentiate the effects of middle ear air volume alteration and Eustachian tube function on barotrauma in guinea pigs exposed to high pressure. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A diving protocol using a pressure chamber was applied to 18 guinea pigs with normal hearing and otoscopic findings (first dive simulation). Ears developing barotrauma were recorded. Three weeks later, after complete recovery was confirmed, bulla obliteration was performed in the left ears of 12 randomly selected guinea pigs (obliteration group), while the right ears underwent bulla opening without obliteration (sham surgery group). After a 2-week wound-healing period, the same diving protocol was repeated (second dive simulation). Otoscopic examination, tympanometry, and auditory brainstem response measurements were then performed, followed by decapitation. In a double-blind design, botulinum toxin was injected into the Eustachian tube muscles on one side of the remaining 6 guinea pigs (botox group), and physiological saline was injected on the contralateral side (saline control group). RESULTS: Some degree of barotrauma was commonly seen in all ears. Within-group comparisons of barotrauma occurrence after the first and second dive simulations showed no significant differences in the obliteration, sham, or saline groups. In contrast, barotrauma developed in all ears in which the Eustachian tube muscles were paralyzed with botulinum toxin. CONCLUSIONS: Isolated reduction of middle ear volume by bulla obliteration did not influence the development of diving-related middle ear barotrauma. In contrast, functional blockade of the Eustachian tube resulted in consistent barotrauma, indicating that Eustachian tube function is the primary determinant of susceptibility to barotrauma during acute pressure changes. Middle ear volume may, therefore, be better interpreted as a long-term marker of Eustachian tube function rather than a direct causal factor.
title: Relative Roles of Middle Ear Bulla Volume and Eustachian Tube Function in Diving-related Barotrauma: An Experimental Pressure Chamber Study in Guinea Pigs

abstract: Abstract Vocalizations are ancient behaviours that require the complex coordination of breath and display. Understanding how laryngeal anatomy shapes vocalization provides insights into this diversity, its mechanisms and their evolution. Rodents are ideal for exploring this variation because of their diverse mechanisms and vocal structures. Here, we describe the laryngeal morphology and sound production mechanisms underlying the vocalizations of Alston’s singing mouse (Scotinomys teguina) and compare these results to those of other vocalizing mammals. We reconstructed the three-dimensional laryngeal morphology with micro-computed tomography, recorded laryngeal sound production using high-speed video and investigated frequency control using surgical ablations. We found that singing mice use a whistle mechanism that uniquely relies on the inflation of an enlarged air sac called the ventral pouch. Song frequency can be controlled by pouch volume, airflow and cricothyroid muscle action. Singing mouse laryngeal morphology and vocal mechanism are distinct from those of other Neotomids; singing mice appear to use inflation-mediated whistles for both distant and close exchanges. Inflatable air sacs have evolved repeatedly for sound modulation and filtering. Our results indicate a novel role for these structures in being required to generate sound. Together, our results expand on an emerging story of how biomechanic and morphological variation contributes to vocal diversity.
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
title: Mechanisms and control of a novel vocalization: the singing mouse song is a whistle that depends on air sac inflation

abstract: Nocturnal conditions impose strong constraints on diurnal species, requiring behavioral adjustments to balance predation risk and social interactions. We investigated how environmental factors shape nocturnal behavior in wintering Common cranes [Grus grus (Linnaeus, 1758)] in central Italy during the 2022-2023 season, using an integrated approach combining camera trapping and acoustic monitoring. We quantified activity, vigilance, display, and vocal behavior in relation to night phase, moon illumination, cloud cover, and seasonal progression. Cranes exhibited high nocturnal activity overall (89.4% ± 2.1% of individuals per night), with 44.8% ± 3.9% showing vigilance. Activity peaked toward morning but decreased significantly with increasing moon illumination, and this effect was partially buffered by cloud cover. Vigilance followed a similar pattern, declining under bright conditions and increasing during darker periods, consistent with antipredatory responses. In contrast, display behavior was positively associated with moon illumination and increased over winter, indicating that cranes exploit illuminated conditions for visually mediated social signaling, possibly in preparation for migration. Vocal activity showed the opposite trend, being higher in darker conditions, indicating its role in maintaining social contact when visual communication is limited. Overall, Common cranes exhibit pronounced nocturnal behavioral flexibility, modulating different behavioral components in response to environmental cues. These findings show how external stimuli can act as selective forces shaping nocturnal strategies in diurnal species.
title: Nocturnal Behavior of Wintering Common Cranes ( Grus grus ) Under Varying Environmental Conditions

abstract: Increasing human presence and activities expose wild animals to persistent disturbances. Disturbed populations often become tolerant towards humans, although the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. We used playback experiments to manipulate perceived level of human disturbance in great tits (Parus major). In the first year, incubating females remained more often on the nest, and parents during brood care exhibited a lower level of vigilance and tended to have shorter return latencies in the human disturbance treatment than in control treatments, demonstrating an increased tolerance. These differences disappeared in the second year. Tolerance was also influenced by distance to roads and the frequency of nest visits by researchers. These results support that behavioural tolerance can quickly emerge by phenotypic plasticity in natural populations, although other mechanisms may also influence behavioural responses after longer exposure to human disturbances, resulting in a complex set of processes involved in the spread of tolerance.
title: Behavioural Effects of Persistent Human Disturbance: A Playback Experiment in a Forest Bird

abstract: Anthropogenic factors such as artificial lighting at night (ALAN) and natural factors including temperature and moonlight can affect the dawn chorus pattern in birds. However, most studies are conducted in temperate regions. We investigated the effect of anthropogenic and natural factors on dawn chorus timing in eight species of bird across Hong Kong, a subtropical city in East Asia. Passive recorders were set at 20 sites and recorded the dawn chorus for 32 days simultaneously. We found dawn chorus started earlier with increased ALAN in six species. The dawn chorus started earlier with higher temperatures in five species; one species delayed dawn chorus on cloudy days, and another species started singing earlier with later dates. Unexpectedly, four species showed a later dawn chorus with higher moon illumination. The effect of ALAN on dawn chorus timing was stronger than other variables, and larger species that started singing earlier were more strongly affected. Our results show that, even in a location with little variation in the time of sunrise across the year, ALAN can cause changes in dawn chorus timing. Our results also highlight another issue; one of the most strongly affected species was the Asian Koel Eudynamys scolopaceus , which has very loud calls. Complaints about the noise of the calls from this genus can be found across Asia and Australia. ALAN could worsen this human–wildlife conflict, as noisy calls occur even earlier in the presence of ALAN.
title: Anthropogenic and natural factors are associated with bird dawn chorus onset in subtropical East Asia

abstract: Birdsong is a key sexual signal that varies substantially among individuals and populations. Understanding whether song similarity reflects genetic similarity is central for evaluating its role in sexual selection, population divergence and evolutionary dynamics, although partial vocal learning can obscure this relationship in many species. Assessing the relationship between song and genetic variation requires accounting for both spatial and temporal heterogeneity in both traits, so despite its importance, the genetic architecture underlying song traits, and in particular song content, remains poorly understood. Here, drawing on 15 years of song recordings and extensive SNP (Single Nucleotide Polymorphism) data, we investigate whether song similarity among males reflects their genome-wide genetic similarity in the collared flycatcher (Ficedula albicollis), a migratory passerine with complex and variable songs. After accounting for geographic and temporal separation, we found no strong association between male song similarity and genome-wide genetic similarity. Moreover, males belonging to the same genetic cluster did not seem to produce more similar songs than those from different clusters. Additionally, genetic distance was unrelated to either geographic or temporal distance, and geographic proximity did not predict song similarity. Instead, song content similarity decreased with increasing temporal separation between recordings, consistent with cultural evolution. Together, these findings indicate that biologically relevant song features are primarily shaped by cultural processes rather than genetic architecture, enabling rapid, flexible responses to environmental changes.
title: Genetic Composition Is Unrelated to Song Content in a Wild Passerine
Occurrence and Whistle Characteristics of Small Odontocetes in Two Coastal Regions of the Sea of Japan
